title: CRLR/120/2012 of SUJAN SINGH and ORS. Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Criminal Revision No. 120 of 2012
Sujan Singh and Others
 ...Revisionists
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand
...Respondent
Mr. L.K. Tiwari, Advocate for the revisionists.
Mr. P.S. Bohra, A.G.A. along with Mr. Siddhartha Bisht, Brief Holder for the State
of Uttarakhand.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J (Oral)
This revision is being decided on a very limited question,
though there are bundle of facts, which has been sought to be argued
by the learned counsel for the parties to the revision.
2. Facts in brief are that, in the proceedings of sessions trial
being Session Trial No. 20 of 2012 (old no. 20/2010) 'State vs. Sujan
Singh and Others', the public prosecutor is said to have filed an
application invoking the provisions contained under Section 216 of
Cr.P.C., which was numbered as Paper No. 57kha before the Sessions
Court praying for an alteration of the charge from Section 306 IPC to
Section 302 IPC.
3. It is based upon the said application and considering the
circumstances and the position of the dead body in which the dead
body was found from the place of incident the Court of District and
Sessions Judge, Tehri Garhwal, by the impugned order, dated
28.05.2012, under challenge has altered the charge from Section 306
IPC to Section 302 IPC, for which the revisionist has to be tried as of
now after the impugned order dated 28.05.2012.
4. After having heard the learned counsel for the parties at
length, the controversy which requires consideration is as to under
which circumstances and conditions the powers under Section 216 of

2
Cr.P.C. could be invoked, and more importantly by whom. For which,
to arrive at logical conclusion the reference to the provisions of
Section 216 of Cr.P.C. is required to be referred, which is quoted
hereunder:
"216. Court may alter charge.
(1) Any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time
before judgment is pronounced.
(2) Every such alteration or addition shall be read and
explained to the accused.
(3) If the alteration or addition to a charge is such that
proceeding immediately with the trial is not likely, in the
opinion of the Court, to prejudice the accused in his defence
or the prosecutor in the conduct of the case, the Court may, in
its discretion, after such alteration or addition has been made,
proceed with the trial as if the altered or added charge had
been the original charge.
(4) If the alteration or addition is such that proceeding
immediately with the trial is likely, in the opinion of the
Court, to prejudice the accused or the prosecutor as aforesaid,
the Court may either direct a new trial or adjourn the trial for
such period as may be necessary.
(5) If the offence stated in the altered or added charge is one
for the prosecution of which previous sanction is necessary,
the case shall not be proceeded with until such sanction is
obtained, unless sanction has been already obtained for a
prosecution on the same facts as those on which the altered or
added charge is founded."
5. If the language of Section 216 of Cr.P.C. itself is taken
into consideration and read to its logical legislative intention, in its
simplicitor interpretation the right to alter the charge itself has been
vested with the "courts" seized with the trial and that is why sub-section (1) of Section 216 of Cr.P.C. has vested the power of
alteration with the court, who could only to alter or add any charge at
any time before the judgment is pronounced. All sub-sections of
Section 216 Cr.P.C. are a follow-up action to sub-section (1) of
Section 216 Cr.P.C., which is to be adhered to after the alteration of
charge under sub-section (1) of Section 216 of Cr.P.C. Meaning
thereby, the principal vesting of power by the statute to alter the
charge has been vested with the Court itself where trial is pending
considering and none of the parties to the proceedings, may it be the
public prosecutor or the accused facing the trial, who has been given a
right to get a charge altered by filing application under Section 216 of
Cr.P.C.

3
6. After having gone through the language of Section 216 of
Cr.P.C., extending the observation to a further extend that, in fact,
Section 216 of Cr.P.C. does not even contemplate or apprehended an
invitation of an application by any of the parties because it is a power,
which has been suo moto vested with the Court itself only, who can
exercise its inherent power in view of provisions contained under
Section 216 of Cr.P.C. to alter the charge and no one else has been
vested with the power to get the charge already framed by filing an
application.
7. In relation thereto, the learned counsel for the revisionist
has placed reliance to the judgment reported in 2017 (3) SCC 347 'P.
Kartikalakshmi vs. Shri Ganesh and Another'. Particularly he has
made reference to paragraph-6 to 8 of the said judgment. In the said
precedent of the Hon'ble Apex Court, in the said judgment it has been
provided that the manner in which the scope of the powers contained
under Section 216 of Cr.P.C. could be exercised to alter a charge, it
could only be exclusively by the Court itself to whom the liberty has
been granted under the said provision, no one else, i.e. any of the
parties to the proceedings, i.e. the accused or the prosecution, can seek
for an addition or an alteration of a charge as a matter of right by
filing an application under Section 216 of Cr.P.C. because if that is
permitted it would lead to a catastrophe situation when the said
provision could be abused by the party to proceedings for their vested
interests.
8. In view of the aforesaid ratio as propounded in
paragraphs- 6, 7 and 8 of the said judgment, which is quoted
hereunder, on that limited premise this revision is allowed:
 "6. Having heard learned Counsel for the respective
parties, we find force in the submission of learned senior
Counsel for Respondent No. 1. Section 216 Code of Criminal
Procedure empowers the Court to alter or add any charge at
any time before the judgment is pronounced. It is now well
settled that the power vested in the Court is exclusive to the
Court and there is no right in any party to seek for such
addition or alteration by filing any application as a matter of

4
right. It may be that if there was an omission in the framing of
the charge and if it comes to the knowledge of the Court
trying the offence, the power is always vested in the Court, as
provided Under Section 216 Code of Criminal Procedure to
either alter or add the charge and that such power is available
with the Court at any time before the judgment is pronounced.
It is an enabling provision for the Court to exercise its power
under certain contingencies which comes to its notice or
brought to its notice. In such a situation if it comes to the
knowledge of the Court that a necessity has arisen for the
charge to be altered or added, it may do so on its own and no
order need be passed for that purpose. After such alteration or
addition when the final decision is rendered, it will be open
for the parties to work out their remedies in accordance with
law.
7. We were taken through Sections 221 & 222 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure in this context. In the light of the
facts involved in this case, we are only concerned with
Section 216 Code of Criminal Procedure We, therefore, do
not propose to examine the implications of the other
provisions to the case on hand. We wish to confine ourselves
to the invocation of Section 216 and rest with that. In the light
of our conclusion that the power of invocation of Section 216
Code of Criminal Procedure is exclusively confined with the
Court as an enabling provision for the purpose of alteration or
addition of any charge at any time before pronouncement of
the judgment, we make it clear that no party, neither de facto
complainant nor the Accused or for that matter the
prosecution has any vested right to seek any addition or
alteration of charge, because it is not provided Under Section
216 Code of Criminal Procedure If such a course to be
adopted by the parties is allowed, then it will be well nigh
impossible for the Criminal Court to conclude its proceedings
and the concept of speedy trial will get jeopardized.
8. In such circumstances, when the application preferred
by the Appellant itself before the Trial Court was not
maintainable, it was not incumbent upon the Trial Court to
pass an order Under Section 216 Code of Criminal Procedure
Therefore, there was no question of the said order being
revisable Under Section 397 Code of Criminal Procedure The
whole proceeding, initiated at the instance of the Appellant,
was not maintainable. Inasmuch as the legal issue had to be
necessarily set right, we are obliged to clarify the law as is
available Under Section 216 Code of Criminal Procedure To
that extent having clarified the legal position, we make it
clear that the whole proceedings initiated at the instance of
the Appellant was thoroughly misconceived and vitiated in
law and ought not to have been entertained by the Trial Court.
As rightly pointed out by the learned senior Counsel for
Respondent No. 1, such a course adopted by the Appellant
and entertained by the Court below has unnecessarily
provided scope for protraction of the proceedings which
ought not to have been allowed by the Court below."
9. The impugned order dated 28.05.2012 altering the charge
from Section 306 IPC to Section 302 IPC, and that too on an

5
application filed by the public prosecutor is inviolation to the
provisions of Section 216 Cr.P.C., and also the ratio of Hon'ble Apex
Court rendered in P. Karthikalakshmi (supra) is quashed. The matter
is remitted back to the Trial Court to decide the trial itself exclusively
on its own merit.
10. However, having held that none of the parties to the trial
can seek the liberty of alteration of the charge under Section 216 of
Cr.P.C., this observation will not lead to an inference that the Trial
Court is being precluded in any manner, whatsoever, to exercise its
power vested with it under law under Section 216 of Cr.P.C. to be
exercised by it.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
 02.12.2019
Pooja
